title: The Summit of the Empty Quarter
premise: When a government survey team vanishes in the Empty Quarter's flooded backcountry, riverboat captain Kestrel Kavanagh is the only pilot willing to run the dying channels to find them. She discovers one survivor, Elias Voss, guarding a discovery the ministry will burn whole towns to bury: an aquifer map proving the concession permits were sold on falsified water surveys. Hunted by the survey team's own security contractor and racing the permit expiration date, Kestrel must smuggle Voss and the evidence downriver while deciding whether survival means silence or truth. In the end she delivers the maps not to the ministry but to the river towns themselves, sacrificing her boat and nearly her life, and finds that belonging was never something the wilderness granted — it was something she built.
about_author: Ansel Pemberton is a former hydrographic surveyor who spent eleven years charting remote river systems before turning to fiction. He writes adventure novels from a houseboat, drawing on firsthand knowledge of what wild water does to people who underestimate it.

chapters.title: Dead Water Season
chapters.summary: Kestrel Kavanagh pilots her aging riverboat through the shrinking channels of the Empty Quarter, ferrying supplies to isolated settlements. A ministry official offers her a lucrative contract: locate the vanished Meridian Survey Team before their concession permits expire. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: restless competence masking her loneliness after years of self-imposed exile from the river towns.

chapters.title: Gear Without Ghosts
chapters.summary: Following the survey team's last logged coordinates, Kestrel finds their abandoned camp — equipment intact, food untouched, no tracks leading out. Only signs of a hurried, deliberate departure by someone who knew they were being watched. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: creeping dread as her expert reading of the land tells her the official story is impossible.

chapters.title: The Man in the Cutbank
chapters.summary: Kestrel discovers Elias Voss, the survey team's cartographer, half-buried in a cutbank, delirious and clutching a waterproof case he refuses to surrender. He claims the rest of the team walked into the marshes at gunpoint, escorted by their own security detail. POV: alternating Kestrel and Voss. Emotional beat: wary alliance between two people who trust nothing.

chapters.title: What the Maps Say
chapters.summary: Voss reveals the case holds aquifer surveys proving the ministry falsified water data to sell concession permits worth fortunes — permits that expire in nineteen days, after which the evidence must reach a tribunal or die with them. POV: Voss. Emotional beat: the weight of knowledge as burden; Voss's guilt over teammates he couldn't save.

chapters.title: Wake on the Horizon
chapters.summary: A fast patrol boat flying contractor colors begins hunting them upriver. Kestrel runs her vessel into a maze of dead channels only she knows, buying distance but damaging her hull. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: fierce joy in her mastery of the river colliding with the realization that mastery alone won't save them.

chapters.title: The Toll of Salt Marsh
chapters.summary: Forced overland through the salt marshes where the survey team disappeared, Kestrel and Voss find the missing members' remains and proof of execution. Voss breaks; Kestrel confronts her own past — the brother she lost to a similar cover-up, the reason she left the towns behind. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: grief transmuted into resolve; the price of survival so far has been silence, and she refuses to pay it again.

chapters.title: Harbor of Strangers
chapters.summary: They reach the river town of Callow's Bend seeking repairs, but the contractor's agents have arrived first, offering the townsfolk a bounty. Kestrel must decide whether to trust the community she abandoned years ago. An old friend, ferryman Odile Marchand, hides them but warns that loyalty here is a currency running thin. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: tentative reconnection; belonging offered and almost refused out of old shame.

chapters.title: Nineteen Days, Spent
chapters.summary: The contractor burns Odile's boathouse as a message, and the permit clock runs down to days. Kestrel learns the tribunal route is compromised — a ministry insider will intercept any official submission. The only path left is the open river, a storm front, and a plan to broadcast the evidence publicly before it can be seized. POV: Voss. Emotional beat: cornered desperation hardening into audacity.

chapters.title: The Running of the Flood
chapters.summary: Climax: Kestrel runs the flooded gorge passage at peak spate — a route considered suicide — with the contractor's boats in pursuit, while Voss transmits the aquifer data to every settlement radio on the river. The patrol boat founders; Kestrel's vessel is wrecked on the far side, and she barely drags Voss ashore. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: terror and transcendence fused; the river forgives nothing, and she asks it for everything anyway.

chapters.title: Where the Water Remembers
chapters.summary: The evidence spreads faster than the ministry can suppress it; permits are suspended pending inquiry, and the river towns rally around Kestrel as one of their own. Boatless but unbroken, she accepts Odile's offer of a place and a new hull to rebuild. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: quiet resolution — power corrupts those who hoard it, but belonging belongs to those who come home.
